title: Structure–Activity Relationships (SAR)
summary: How systematic structural changes reveal what matters for activity.

lessons.title: What SAR is

levels.kid:
A tiny change to a molecule can make a big change to what it does. Imagine two keys that look nearly the same: one opens a lock easily, while the other doesn't fit at all.

Chemists make families of similar molecules and **test** them. They change one piece at a time, like swapping a small knob on the key. Then they compare how well each one works. The pattern they find is called **structure–activity relationship**, or **SAR**.

SAR helps them figure out which pieces are important for grabbing a target and which can be changed to make a medicine safer. They never assume a molecule works just because it looks like another one: they check it with an experiment.
levels.hs:
**Structure–activity relationship (SAR)** links changes in chemical structure to changes in biological activity. In a medicinal chemistry project, scientists make a series of related compounds, measure their ability to affect a target, and look for patterns.

Picture a molecule with a ring, an amine and a flexible tail. Changing the ring substituent might raise potency. Removing the amine might destroy activity because it supplied an important ionic interaction. Shortening the tail might improve selectivity. Comparing the measured results tells chemists which features matter.

The crucial rule is **change one thing at a time when possible**. If you replace the ring, tail and amine simultaneously, you cannot tell which edit caused the change. Use the same assay conditions for every analog, including controls, and repeat unexpected results.

Activity is often reported as IC50 (concentration causing 50% inhibition), EC50 (concentration causing 50% effect) or a binding affinity such as Kd. A lower IC50 often means stronger inhibition in that specific assay, but it does not by itself prove greater benefit in a person. Solubility, cell permeability, toxicity and metabolic stability all matter too.
levels.college:
**SAR as a controlled experiment.** A congeneric series shares a scaffold and varies substituents at specified positions. Potency metrics include pIC50 = −log10(IC50 in molar units), pEC50 and pKd; each unit of pIC50 corresponds to a tenfold concentration shift. IC50 depends on substrate concentration for competitive enzyme inhibitors (Cheng–Prusoff), unlike Ki under its defined model. Comparing IC50s measured under different protocols is unsafe.

**Interpretation.** Removing a carbonyl that accepts a hydrogen bond may reduce affinity, but the cause could also be a conformational change, altered protonation or solubility. SAR establishes empirical associations; crystallography, biophysics and thermodynamic analysis strengthen mechanistic claims. A flat SAR region—many analogs having similar activity—signals a solvent-exposed substituent or an assay-limited dynamic range; it may provide room to optimize ADME.

**Beyond potency.** Track ligand efficiency (LE ≈ 1.37 × pKd / heavy-atom count in kcal/mol per atom at room temperature, a useful shorthand with convention-dependent constant) and lipophilic ligand efficiency (LLE = pIC50 − logD). The precise LE formula is −ΔG / heavy-atom count; −ΔG from Kd in molar units, not IC50 unless assumptions hold. Increased potency from adding hydrophobic bulk may lose LLE and worsen solubility or hERG liability.

**Design loop.** Hypothesis → synthesize a small analog set → test potency and selectivity → inspect assay quality → measure ADME → revise. Never extrapolate an SAR trend indefinitely.
levels.phd:
**Causal versus correlational SAR.** Medicinal chemistry uses interventions on molecules, but each intervention changes several coupled latent variables—conformation, hydration, pKa, tautomer distribution, logD and chemical stability. Even a single-atom edit is not a controlled change in only one physical property. A potency gain after adding fluorine may reflect electrostatics, conformational preorganization, altered pKa, displacement of water or different assay recovery. Binding free energy decompositions into enthalpy and entropy are experimentally measurable by ITC but their molecular assignment is nonunique.

**Assay comparability.** In biochemical enzyme assays, IC50 changes with substrate concentration for competitive inhibitors. In cell assays, uptake, efflux, protein binding and target abundance influence apparent potency. Time-dependent inhibition makes equilibrium IC50 unsuitable. Orthogonal biophysical assays (SPR, ITC, DSF) and target engagement (CETSA, NanoBRET) check whether a striking SAR is target-mediated rather than an assay artefact.

**Statistics.** Replicate variability defines whether a twofold change is meaningful. If assay standard deviation is 0.2 log units, a shift of 0.1 pIC50 is weak evidence. Bayesian sequential design can allocate synthesis toward information gain rather than merely the current highest potency.

**Multiparameter landscapes.** SAR is not one curve: potency, selectivity, permeability, metabolic stability and safety liabilities form a Pareto frontier. A compound is dominated if another is at least as good on every property and better on one. Teams choose trade-offs consistent with target product profiles, not just the top binding score. An orthogonal assay helps separate true target engagement from a platform-specific signal.
levels.expert:
**How a lead team reads its SAR table.** Begin with assay provenance. Were analogs tested in the same run, with the same ATP or substrate concentration, target construct and curve-fitting criteria? Confirm a surprising fivefold shift in independent material. Check concentration–response curves and counterscreens for aggregation, fluorescence interference and cytotoxicity. A beautiful SAR based on bad assay data is not SAR.

**Annotate each analog by intent.** A fluorine might test an oxidation hypothesis, a methyl an occupied pocket, an N-methyl an H-bond donor, a pyridine a solubility hypothesis. If a compound improves biochemical potency but loses cellular activity, investigate permeability, efflux and unbound concentration rather than concluding the binding model failed.

**Decision rule.** Prioritize a set of candidates, not a single winner. For example, one compound tests high potency, another better metabolic stability and a third selectivity. Keep structure and batch IDs connected to validated purity and stereochemical assignments.

**Pitfalls.** A presumed inactive analog may actually be insoluble at test concentrations; a racemate may hide one powerful enantiomer; small IC50 differences near the assay's noise floor invite false narratives. Independent resynthesis and dose–response replication are cheap relative to taking a false mechanism into animal studies.

**Communicating SAR.** Report actual potency and uncertainty, not just arrows. Mark an improvement as local to its scaffold and assay. Show potency alongside LLE, fu, permeability and off-target selectivity so decision-makers see the whole landscape.

keyPoints: SAR links systematic structural edits to measured biological activity.
One-change comparisons isolate hypotheses but cannot isolate every physicochemical cause.
Lower IC50 indicates greater potency within a comparable assay, not necessarily clinical efficacy.
pIC50 = −log10(IC50 in molar units); one unit is a tenfold difference.
Always optimize selectivity and ADME alongside potency.

examples.tr: A fall in potency suggests the amine helps binding; pKa or solubility may also change.
Tenfold lower concentration is one pIC50 unit higher in the same assay.

lessons.title: Designing analog series

levels.kid:
Suppose you are making a key for a lock. You could try a different tooth, then a longer handle, then a new material. But if you change everything at once, how will you know what helped?

Chemists make an **analog series**: a row of similar molecules with one small change in each. They plan the changes before making them. One might add a tiny methyl piece; another might swap one atom for fluorine; a third might move a piece to another spot on a ring.

After testing each molecule, they compare results. A good series answers a question, even if none of the new molecules is the best medicine. A failed experiment still teaches them where the lock is tight.
levels.hs:
An **analog series** is a planned set of molecules built around a shared scaffold, with controlled changes in one or a few places. Scientists use it to learn which features improve potency, selectivity and drug-like properties.

A useful series tests a hypothesis. Suppose a lead has a phenyl ring. Make versions with fluorine at the ortho, meta and para positions to ask whether the binding pocket favors a particular direction. Then try a methyl group to test whether a small hydrophobic pocket exists. Swapping phenyl for pyridine may improve solubility and change binding.

Also try **deletion analogs**: remove a hydrogen-bond donor or shorten a tail. If activity collapses, that group may be necessary; if it doesn't, it may be removable to improve ADME.

**Keep comparisons fair:** use the same assay, check compound identity and purity, and include replicates. A lower IC50 for one analog may mean better binding, or simply better solubility in the assay. Test both.

Choose a few **informative compounds**, not hundreds of random variations. A deliberately inactive control can help reveal whether an apparent effect is specific to the target.
levels.college:
**Design dimensions.** At each substituent site, probe steric volume (H→Me→Et), electronics (F, Cl, OMe, CF3, CN), polarity (OH, NH2, pyridyl) and topology (ortho/meta/para; ring size). Vary one dimension initially, then test interactions by combining favorable substituents. A complete factorial design can be expensive; fractional factorial designs give information with fewer compounds.

**Hypothesis-first series.** If a crystallographic pocket is hydrophobic, scan small alkyl and halogen groups. If a solvent-exposed region is available, try polar substituents to lower logD while preserving potency. If an aromatic ring is metabolized, test pyridine or fluorination. The Topliss decision tree for phenyl substituents is an early heuristic for exploring lipophilic, electronic and steric effects; it is not a universal recipe.

**Buildable chemistry matters.** Parallel synthesis is useful only if products meet identity and purity criteria. Synthetic accessibility, regioisomer separation and stereochemistry constrain the design; a fast, reliable late-stage diversification reaction can produce high-information matched pairs.

**Read all endpoints.** Record biochemical potency, cellular target engagement, selectivity, solubility, permeability and microsomal stability. A gain in potency purchased entirely by increased logD may be a bad trade. Include a reference compound in each assay batch to control drift.

**Decision making.** An analog that disproves the binding hypothesis is a useful result. Update the model and select the next series based on uncertainty rather than blindly appending bigger groups.
levels.phd:
**Experimental design in chemical space.** Analog series are sequential interventions with multiple correlated effects. Orthogonal substituent sets and factorial designs help disentangle main effects from interactions. A 2×2 cycle compares four compounds: parent, edit A, edit B and A+B; if ΔΔG(A+B) differs from the sum of single-edit ΔΔGs, the edits are energetically coupled. Double-mutant cycles can also pair ligand modification with protein mutation to probe a specific interaction, but structural rearrangement can confound interpretations.

**Sampling and uncertainty.** With limited synthesis capacity, Bayesian optimization balances expected improvement against exploration of poorly sampled regions; active learning chooses compounds that reduce uncertainty. Pareto optimization handles potency, selectivity and ADME together. The uncertainty of each endpoint should be carried into decision rules, and assay-to-assay drift is controlled with bridge compounds.

**Stereochemical dimensions.** A racemate is two compounds for SAR purposes. Isolating enantiomers may reveal a large eudismic ratio (affinity difference) that averaging conceals. Atropisomers and conformationally restricted analogs can likewise produce distinct activity.

**Molecular matched pairs.** If possible, choose analogs that differ by a single well-defined transformation (for example H→F) in the same local context. Compound pairs formed by changing several sites simultaneously are less interpretable.

**Real-world attrition.** Building a model requires negatives, not only the best positives. Record synthesis failures and insoluble compounds without treating them as inactive. A prioritization framework that treats missing measurements as zero activity creates severe selection bias. Chemical tractability and turnaround time also determine which experiment is actually worth doing next.
levels.expert:
**Running the design meeting.** State each proposed compound's job before anyone makes it: "tests whether the para pocket accepts halogen," "moves polar nitrogen toward solvent," or "tests whether a labile benzylic methyl is needed." Put the proposed outcome, planned assay and a backup hypothesis next to its structure. Limit a batch to compounds that can be made and tested promptly.

**First-pass triage.** Confirm synthetic route, expected stereochemistry, salt form and analytical method. Same batch of protein, substrate concentration and reference compound should anchor the potency comparison. Retest meaningful activity jumps in orthogonal assays. Keep the dose–response curve, not only an IC50 number.

**Avoid overclaiming.** A para-fluoro analog that gains potency and stability is exciting, but don't assign both to a new contact without structure or binding data. Fluorine could prevent metabolism while changing pKa or conformation. Also do not conflate a cell potency gain with a target-affinity gain: free intracellular concentration may have changed.

**Next-cycle choices.** If all analogs retain potency despite varied solvent-facing groups, use that site to improve solubility or add a linker. If a steric scan reveals a narrow optimum, preserve it while varying another vector. If results are noisy, improve assay reproducibility before making dozens more analogs.

**Ethos.** The best series is a decision engine: it can kill a bad scaffold early, map an interaction accurately or uncover an ADME rescue. Publishing only the winning analogs hides the information that drove the decision.

keyPoints: An analog series changes a shared scaffold systematically to test hypotheses.
Scan steric size, electronics, polarity and substituent position.
Deletion analogs test whether a group is needed, but activity loss may have indirect causes.
Fair comparison requires matching assay conditions, compound identity and purity.
Use informative negatives and measure ADME, not just potency.

lessons.title: Activity cliffs

levels.kid:
Two mountains can look close together on a map, but one ends in a sudden cliff. Molecules sometimes do that too.

Two almost-matching molecules may work very differently. A tiny new piece on one molecule can make it grip the target much better—or make it stop fitting altogether. Chemists call this an **activity cliff**.

Imagine a key that fits a lock. Put a small bump in exactly the wrong spot, and the key jams. Put it in a tiny empty notch, and suddenly the key turns smoothly.

A cliff is exciting because it shows where the lock is picky. But chemists repeat the test before celebrating: a broken sample or a noisy test can make a fake cliff.
levels.hs:
An **activity cliff** is a large change in biological activity caused by a small structural change. Two molecules that differ only by a methyl group, a fluorine or the position of a ring nitrogen might have a tenfold or even much larger potency difference.

Why can this happen? A tiny group may fill an otherwise empty binding pocket, push out an unfavorable water molecule, force a useful conformation, or clash with the protein. Moving one hydrogen-bond donor may break a critical interaction. Enantiomers—mirror-image molecules—can also bind differently to a chiral protein.

The "**magic methyl**" effect describes a methyl group causing an unexpectedly large gain in activity. It isn't magic: the group can fill a pocket, change the molecule's preferred shape or displace ordered water.

But not every sudden jump is real. Assay noise, different solubility, protein aggregation or wrong compound identity can mimic an activity cliff. Repeat the assay, check purity and measure binding independently.

Cliffs are especially useful for learning where a target is intolerant of change; they warn that smoothly interpolating between similar molecules is not always reliable.
levels.college:
**Definition.** An activity cliff is a pair of highly similar structures with a disproportionately large potency difference, commonly a ≥10-fold shift (≥1 pIC50 unit). Similarity must be specified: a matched molecular pair differs by one localized transformation; a fingerprint similarity threshold can identify broader cliffs but may miss 3D effects.

**Mechanisms.** A ligand edit can disrupt a key salt bridge, hydrogen bond or tightly packed contact; shift a tautomer or protonation state; preorganize a binding conformation; or replace a high-energy water. A methyl group may exploit a hydrophobic pocket and reduce the conformational entropy cost of binding. Stereochemical inversion is small in 2D connectivity but can radically change 3D fit.

**Quantifying cliffs.** Structure–activity landscape index, SALI = |Ai − Aj| / (1 − Sij), where A is activity on a consistent logarithmic scale and S is structural similarity from 0 to 1. A high SALI marks a strong change between similar structures, but it becomes unstable when S approaches 1 and depends on fingerprint choice.

**Validation.** Verify purity, solubility, assay dynamic range, curve shape and replicate precision. For apparent enzyme-inhibition cliffs, rule out time-dependent kinetics, redox cycling and aggregation. Binding studies or co-crystal structures can test a mechanistic hypothesis.

**Design consequence.** Cliffs are information-rich but hazardous to smooth QSAR models: tiny edits can invalidate interpolation. Map the local region with additional analogs before generalizing.
levels.phd:
**Energy scale.** A tenfold equilibrium binding change corresponds to ΔΔG ≈ RT ln 10 ≈ 1.36 kcal/mol at 298 K—small on the scale of individual molecular interactions. A seemingly dramatic potency cliff can therefore arise from a modest net shift in desolvation, protein rearrangement and conformational entropy. Conversely, tiny geometric clashes can trigger a binding-mode switch with far larger energetic consequences.

**Water thermodynamics.** Displacing a constrained, high-energy water from a hydrophobic subpocket can strongly improve affinity, while removing a water that bridges ligand and protein can reduce it. WaterMap and GIST attempt to estimate these effects; crystallographic absence of a water alone does not prove an energetically favorable displacement.

**Conformational and stereochemical cliffs.** Fluorine adjacent to an amide or amine can favor a particular rotamer or shift pKa. A single methyl can enforce a dihedral, preorganizing the bioactive conformer. Atropisomers that interconvert slowly may have substantially different affinities. Cliffs are therefore better understood as discontinuities in a high-dimensional thermodynamic landscape than exceptions to a simple additivity rule.

**Data pathology.** Apparent cliffs can be invented by mixing Ki, IC50 and cell EC50 from noncomparable experiments, or by treating censored values (>highest tested concentration) as exact. SALI magnifies activity measurement error near similarity 1. A credible cliff has independent resynthesis and repeat, preferably with orthogonal binding measurements.

**Machine learning.** Fingerprint-based regressors tend to smooth locally and miss cliffs. Contrastive learning, local models and uncertainty estimation help prioritize apparent cliffs for experimental follow-up rather than claiming prediction certainty.
levels.expert:
**What to do when you see a cliff.** First check the physical samples: identity by LC-MS/NMR, stereochemical assignment and purity, then solubility and free concentration at the top assay point. Repeat full concentration–response curves side by side with the same protein lot. An oddly steep Hill slope, fluorescence interference or colloidal aggregation makes an apparent cliff suspect.

**Then build a mechanism.** Get a co-crystal or cryo-EM structure if feasible; if not, measure Kd by SPR/ITC, run competitive-binding experiments and make one or two rescue analogs. If methylation improved potency, test ethyl and cyclopropyl at the same position: a pocket-size optimum supports a steric hypothesis; a flat trend suggests exposure or assay effects.

**Project impact.** A real cliff is both opportunity and warning. It can map an important anchor or uncover a new binding pose, but a series on a narrow cliff can be brittle: minor impurities, pH shifts or stereochemical instability may matter. Record compound concentrations and assay limits explicitly so future modelers do not mistake censored results for exact potencies.

**Thermodynamic humility.** A 10-fold Kd difference is only about 1.4 kcal/mol in binding free energy at room temperature. Structural pictures tempt people to assign the full change to one contact, yet solvation and protein rearrangement contribute. Keep explanations conditional until discriminating experiments support them. If binding measurements disagree with functional potency, look for slow binding kinetics, receptor reserve or permeability effects before declaring the cliff real.

keyPoints: Activity cliff = high structural similarity but a disproportionately large activity difference.
A tenfold affinity change is about 1.36 kcal/mol at room temperature.
Possible causes: steric clash, conformational preorganization, protonation or water displacement.
SALI quantifies activity difference relative to structural similarity but depends on the metric.
Repeat surprising cliffs and rule out assay or solubility artifacts.

lessons.title: Matched molecular pairs

levels.kid:
Imagine two cookies baked from the same recipe. One has a cherry and the other has a blueberry. If everyone likes one more, you can ask what the fruit changed.

Chemists do this with molecules. They put two nearly identical molecules side by side, differing in **one small spot**. That is a **matched pair**. Maybe one has a hydrogen atom and the other a fluorine. Then they measure both in the same test.

The difference can teach them about activity, dissolving in water or how fast the body breaks the molecules apart. But a trick that helped one pair may not help another pair. Every molecule has its own surroundings, just as a cherry may taste different in a chocolate cookie.
levels.hs:
A **matched molecular pair (MMP)** consists of two compounds differing by one well-defined, localized structural transformation: for example hydrogen→fluorine at one ring position, or methyl→hydroxymethyl on one side chain.

The measured difference between the pair (ΔpIC50, ΔlogD, Δsolubility or Δclearance) helps estimate what that change did **in that scaffold context**. Many pairs across a database can give a rough average of what a transformation usually does. Fluorination may block a metabolic site, while replacing a phenyl ring with pyridine often lowers lipophilicity and improves solubility.

But a transformation's effect is **context-dependent**. A fluorine added to a tight pocket may improve binding; at a different position it may clash. Moving a nitrogen into a ring can change pKa, which affects both binding and permeability.

Matched pairs are useful for planning analogs because they translate a vague idea—"make it more soluble"—into a testable chemical edit. Always check the assay's error, compound identity and whether the pair truly differs at just one site.
levels.college:
**Definition and computation.** MMP analysis identifies molecule pairs differing by a single localized transformation. Algorithms fragment molecules at acyclic bonds (for example Hussain–Rea fragmentation), index shared cores and compare substituted fragments. Ring edits and multiple attachment points require care because atom mapping and regiochemistry can be ambiguous.

**Property differences.** For paired compounds A→B, calculate ΔpIC50, ΔlogD, Δsolubility, Δclearance and ΔhERG potency under comparable assays. Across many matched pairs, report distributions and confidence intervals, not just a mean. A skewed distribution may hide that the transformation helps only in certain contexts.

**Examples.** H→F at a benzylic position may slow metabolism by eliminating a labile C–H but can also change local polarity or conformation. Phenyl→pyridyl often lowers logD and improves aqueous solubility if the new nitrogen is not protonated, yet may add an aldehyde oxidase liability. N-methylation removes an H-bond donor and can improve permeability while damaging potency or solubility.

**Causality limits.** A one-site edit still perturbs multiple physicochemical properties. Matched pairs estimate a local transformation effect, not an isolated physical mechanism. Larger transformations are less transferable; assay noise and batch effects can reverse small apparent trends.

**Use in design.** Filter database pairs by the same target, similar local environment and assay protocol. Choose edits whose possible gains justify their synthesis and test them prospectively.
levels.phd:
**MMP estimands.** A matched pair defines a finite chemical intervention T on a particular core. The outcome Δy = y(T(x)) − y(x) is context-conditioned; it is not a universal coefficient for T. Transform distributions can be hierarchical: global prior effect, target-specific effect, local-scaffold effect, residual. Pooling all H→F pairs can induce Simpson's paradox if scaffold families have different baselines or selection biases.

**Activity cliffs and non-additivity.** When an MMP shows a large ΔpIC50, inspect conformational and tautomeric consequences before attributing it to a local contact. Applying two transformations sequentially may fail to yield the sum of their observed effects; matched molecular **series** and matched-pair networks reveal epistasis and target-specific context.

**Statistical hygiene.** Potency entries from distinct protocols should not be combined without calibration. Handle censored measurements (IC50 above the assay ceiling) as inequalities; replacing them with the ceiling biases Δ estimates. Shared molecules in multiple pairs make observations statistically dependent, so naive standard errors understate uncertainty.

**Property-space confounding.** A pyridine swap changes H-bond acceptor count, dipole, pKa, logD, aqueous solubility, CNS penetration and aldehyde oxidase susceptibility. MMPs reveal the net local outcome but do not identify the mechanism without orthogonal experiments.

**Predictive use.** MMP rules often outperform global QSAR for a close analog and may extrapolate poorly to a new scaffold. Report both direction probability and effect-size distribution. Leave-one-scaffold-out validation is more realistic than a random split for gauging transfer to a novel series.
levels.expert:
**At the design table.** Search the project's measured pair history before proposing the obvious edit. A para-fluoro substitution may have improved stability in two analogs but killed potency in three others because the pocket is crowded. Use the **local** series, not an industry-wide average, to set the prior.

**Data discipline.** Store core, transformation, stereochemistry, salts, assay date, actual numeric result and detection limit. Pairs with different assay versions require a bridge compound or should be analyzed separately. Plot the pair's entire property vector, not only ΔpIC50. A potency gain accompanied by tenfold worse solubility might be a net loss.

**Design examples.** For high CYP clearance at a benzylic site, test H→F or benzylic methyl→CF3 alongside a polarity-lowering edit; identify metabolites afterward to check for metabolic switching. For low solubility, try ring N insertion or a polar solvent-facing group, but monitor permeability and AO clearance.

**Failure modes.** Fluorination is not reliably an oxidation fix if the enzyme attacks another site; pyridine is not guaranteed to rescue solubility if crystal packing becomes stronger. A pair found only because one compound was selected for testing may be biased by project triage. Prospective synthesis of a predicted pair is the cleanest validation.

**Practical payoff.** MMPA converts an unstructured chemistry database into a ranked menu of transformations with expected trade-offs and uncertainty, while leaving the ultimate decision to direct experiments in the actual scaffold. Before generalizing a transformation, specify the scaffold neighborhood, assay uncertainty and which endpoints were observed rather than imputed.

keyPoints: MMP = two compounds differing by one localized structural transformation.
Compare matched compounds under the same assay to estimate the transformation's local effect.
The same edit can help in one scaffold and hurt in another.
One-site changes still alter several physical properties; they do not prove mechanism.
Summarize distributions and uncertainty, not only average effects.

lessons.title: Free–Wilson & QSAR basics

levels.kid:
Suppose you want to predict how good a new key will be before making it. You remember that one bump helped, and one notch hurt. You add their scores to make a guess.

Chemists sometimes do something like that for medicines. They use the test results for molecules they already made to build a **model**. The model tries to predict how a new molecule will work from its parts and properties.

This is called **QSAR**, a way to connect molecule numbers to activity numbers. Models can save time, but they can make mistakes. If two changes together behave differently from either alone, simple adding fails. So chemists test the model on molecules it has never seen.
levels.hs:
**Quantitative structure–activity relationships (QSAR)** use numbers describing molecules to predict measured activity. Descriptors can be size, lipophilicity (logD), electronic properties, shape or a fingerprint encoding structural patterns.

A classic idea, the **Free–Wilson model**, assigns a contribution to each substituent at a position on a shared scaffold. The predicted activity is a baseline plus the contributions of the substituents present. It works best when their effects are approximately additive; it struggles when two groups interact or the protein changes shape.

**Hansch analysis** is another early QSAR approach. It relates activity to properties such as hydrophobicity (π), electronic effects (Hammett σ) and steric size (Es). Too little or too much lipophilicity can be bad, producing a curved relation rather than a straight line.

Modern QSAR may use machine learning, but its value depends on good data and fair testing. Split data into training and test sets, preferably by scaffold or time so the model cannot memorize near-identical compounds. Never treat a high training score as proof that it predicts new chemistry.
levels.college:
**Free–Wilson analysis.** For a congeneric series with positions i and substituents j, model log activity as A = μ + Σ aij xij, where xij is 1 if substituent j occurs at position i, else 0. It estimates additive contributions but cannot predict a substituent absent from training and becomes unstable when combinations are confounded. Interaction terms can capture non-additivity, at the cost of more data.

**Hansch QSAR.** pIC50 (or log 1/C) is regressed on hydrophobic substituent constant π (relative to H), Hammett electronic σ and Taft steric Es, sometimes with a π² term for an optimal lipophilicity. Coefficients describe association within that series, not universal mechanistic laws. Correlated descriptors make interpretation fragile.

**Modern models.** 2D fingerprints, physicochemical descriptors and 3D fields feed linear regression, random forests, gradient boosting, graph networks or 3D-QSAR approaches such as CoMFA. Model quality is assessed on compounds kept out of training, using RMSE/MAE, rank correlation or classification metrics suited to the task.

**Validation.** Random splitting of close analogs yields inflated estimates for novel scaffolds. Scaffold split and prospective or temporal validation better mimic discovery. Define an **applicability domain**: predictions far from known chemistry are less reliable. Watch assay heterogeneity, censored values, label leakage and imbalanced classes.

**Use.** QSAR ranks compounds for synthesis; it does not replace experimental binding, ADME and safety assays.
levels.phd:
**Model identifiability.** In Free–Wilson regression, dummy variables for all substituents plus an intercept are collinear; choose a reference group or impose a sum-to-zero constraint. Sparse substitution matrices yield poorly estimated coefficients. Interaction terms can model epistasis but create combinatorial demand. A regularized hierarchical model can partially pool estimates by chemical similarity.

**Hansch caveats.** π, σ and Es correlate in common substituent sets, making regression coefficients unstable. Quadratic logP terms encode an empirical optimum often arising from a balance of permeability and solubility; they do not identify a unique biochemical mechanism. The Y-randomization test (shuffle activities, refit) exposes chance correlations when the dataset is small relative to descriptors.

**Validation pitfalls.** A random split on highly congeneric molecules leaks local SAR into the test set, overstating out-of-series performance. Scaffold or time splits are stronger but can be pessimistic for within-series prioritization; evaluate on the actual use case. Nested cross-validation prevents hyperparameter tuning on the final test set. Keep censored assay results as intervals, not exact labels.

**Uncertainty.** Ensembles and conformal prediction can quantify empirical error; calibration must be checked on independent scaffolds. A model can be accurate on average yet dangerously overconfident near activity cliffs. Applicability domain may use fingerprint distance or latent-space density, but no distance metric fully predicts reliability.

**3D-QSAR.** CoMFA grids depend strongly on ligand alignment and conformation. Alignment that uses the endpoint or post-hoc selection creates leakage. A co-crystal template and prospective validation are more persuasive than a visually appealing field map.
levels.expert:
**How to deploy QSAR without fooling the team.** First harmonize assay data: target construct, substrate, readout, units and dates. Keep IC50 values as censored where the assay never reached 50% inhibition. Assign train/test by compound registration date for a realistic prospective backtest, and separately test a new scaffold if that is the intended use.

**Choose the simplest model that works.** A Free–Wilson table or matched-pair average often beats a giant graph network for a small congeneric series because it is inspectable and admits uncertainty. Machine learning is valuable for larger, diverse data only when clean labels and an honest independent set exist.

**Communication rule.** Deliver a predicted range and applicability warning, not a falsely precise IC50. When two candidate compounds have overlapping uncertainty intervals, prioritize synthesis by synthetic accessibility, ADME hypothesis and information gain. Check whether the model systematically underpredicts activity cliffs or overpredicts high-logD analogs.

**Operational checks.** Freeze data preprocessing and model version, monitor performance as new measured analogs arrive, and flag distribution drift. If a model's top suggestions are insoluble or unstable, add those endpoints to the decision rule rather than optimizing potency alone.

**The practical point:** QSAR is a tool for deciding what to make next; it is not a substitute for controlled experiments or a guaranteed explanation of why a molecule works. A useful model should improve the next synthesis decision against a transparent baseline such as nearest-neighbor SAR, not merely fit history.

keyPoints: Free–Wilson predicts log activity from additive substituent contributions.
Hansch QSAR relates activity to hydrophobic, electronic and steric descriptors.
Modern QSAR uses fingerprints or physicochemical features plus statistical models.
Scaffold/temporal and prospective tests expose overoptimistic random-split performance.
Predictions need an applicability domain and honest uncertainty.
